title: Slide a fixed angle against two pins and its tip draws part of a circle

cover.alt: A hand holds a pencil at the corner of a clear acrylic set square that rests against two small pins on a white board marked 90°.

body: Push two pins into a board and slide a rigid angle against them, so that each arm always touches one pin. However you move it, the corner stays on a single **arc of a circle**. That is the **inscribed angle theorem**: every point on the arc sees the two pins under the same angle, which is exactly half the angle they make at the circle’s centre. Its oldest known appearance is in Book 3 of Euclid’s *Elements*.

slides.alt: A hand slides a clear acrylic angle against two pins on a white board while a pencil at its corner draws a curve: a semicircle for 90 degrees, then a bigger arc for 60 degrees and a smaller one for 120 degrees.
slides.caption: An exhibit in Matemateca, São Paulo: a rigid angle slides against two pins, and a pencil at its corner draws an arc. 90° gives a semicircle, 60° a bigger arc and 120° a smaller one.

slides.heading: Which arc does each corner draw?
slides.explanation: The sharper the corner, the bigger the arc: a right angle fits exactly in a semicircle, a sharper one in a bigger arc, a wider one in a smaller arc.

slides.label: the angle the two pins make at the circle’s centre, compared with the angle at the corner
slides.text: Both angles open onto the same two points, so fixing the corner angle fixes the circle’s centre too. That is why the corner can only move along one arc.

slides.heading: The right-angle case
slides.text: With a 90° corner, the pins mark the two ends of a diameter and the corner traces a semicircle. That special case is Thales’s theorem: an angle drawn in a semicircle is always a right angle. Another consequence: in any four-sided shape whose corners all lie on a circle, opposite angles add up to 180°.

slides.question: A corner on the arc measures 35°. What angle do the same two points make at the circle’s centre?
slides.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle on the same arc, so 2 × 35° = 70°.
